title: ZenHealth - latency & throughput profiling discussion
next_steps: Redwood to run token/sec microbenchmarks on their sample model and share spreadsheet
Share SOC2/security whitepaper and VPC deployment checklist
Schedule dedicated private deployment deep-dive with ZenHealth infra team next week
Provide cost estimate for 99th and p95 latency SLOs at target concurrency
action_items: Diego - run streaming + non-streaming p95 token/sec benchmarks using 8k context by 2025-03-18
Maya - send security pack (SOC2, ISO) and contract template by 2025-03-14
Omar - share current traffic profile (p50/p95 tokens per request, concurrency peaks) by 2025-03-15
summary: Discovery focused on p95 latency targets and throughput for a hybrid deployment. ZenHealth needs sub-300ms p95 for short prompt completions at 200 concurrent users, and sustained token/sec for streaming clinical note generation. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, KV/prefix caching, batching, model variants and fallback, and security requirements (VPC/KMS/SOC2). Next step: Redwood to run token/sec microbenchmarks and share results plus security docs; schedule deep-dive for private deployment sizing.
transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone — thanks for carving out time. We have Maya and Diego from Redwood, hi team from ZenHealth?
[00:00:05] Lena Park: Hi, Lena here. We have Omar, Sasha and Ravi as well. Thanks for doing this — we wanted to walk through latency/throughput constraints so we can pick Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.
[00:00:14] Maya Chen: Great, that's exactly what we hoped to cover. Quick agenda: get your traffic profile, p95 targets, discuss streaming vs non-streaming use cases, then constraints (VPC, KMS, compliance), and next steps. Sound good?
[00:00:23] Omar Rahman: Yep. To be clear — we're running two main workloads. One is short clinical triage answers (avg 40 tokens, often must be <300ms p95). The other is longer note generation for visit summaries that use streaming and average 800–2k tokens but can tolerate higher latency.
[00:00:36] Diego Alvarez: Nice — two different profiles. For the short path, is 300ms p95 firm? That is aggressive for many models on standard hosted stacks.
[00:00:44] Lena Park: It's our target. Front-end rules want sub-300ms p95 for the suggested completion so clinicians don't feel lag. We can accept occasional spikes but want 95th under 300ms for the 40-token flow at steady 200 concurrency across regions.
[00:00:57] Priya Nair: 200 concurrent users — do you mean 200 concurrent model requests, or 200 UI users with bursts?
[00:01:03] Ravi Patel: 200 concurrent requests at peak, sustained for roughly 10 minute windows after clinic start times. Baseline concurrency is ~30.
[00:01:11] Diego Alvarez: Ok. A few things to clarify: model family, max context, and whether streaming is used for the short completion. Because 40 tokens non-streaming and streaming difference is small but overhead of streaming commits you to a lesser tail. Also network distance matters for p95.
[00:01:25] Sasha Green: We're evaluating open models — likely an optimized Llama2-70B quantized variant or Mistral family. We can choose model variants if you advise. For short completions we prefer a smaller low-latency variant.
[00:01:35] Maya Chen: Exactly. Our recommendation often is to use a low-latency model variant for the small completions (e.g., distilled or 7B-class) and route long-form streaming to larger models with KV cache. That minimizes cost and helps hit p95.
[00:01:44] Omar Rahman: The question is — can Hosted meet our 300ms p95 at 200 concurrent requests? Or do we need Dedicated? And what about Private in our VPC?
[00:01:53] Diego Alvarez: Short answer: Hosted can sometimes hit that if you pick a tuned small model + edge routing in region, and if we reserve capacity (bursting aside). But at sustained 200 concurrency you probably need Dedicated capacity to guarantee p95. Private adds network and ops overhead — achieving 300ms p95 in an on-prem VPC path depends on your egress and NICs.
[00:02:08] Maya Chen: We'll quantify. We should run token/sec microbenchmarks with your target model and context length. Diego can run a streaming vs non-streaming sweep and produce p50/p95/p99 numbers for tokens/sec and per-request latency.
[00:02:20] Diego Alvarez: I'll run tests: 7b low-latency, 13b quantized, and a 70b quantized model for longer flows, both streaming and non-streaming. I'll include different batch sizes (1, 4, 8) and KV-cached warm/unwarm runs.
[00:02:33] Lena Park: Also include warm start vs cold. Our traffic is bursty — initial requests at start of clinic are cold. We need to understand cold-start tail.
[00:02:41] Priya Nair: Good point. Also do we want to see results for continuous batching at your side? Redwood runtime does adaptive batching that tries to maximize throughput while preserving latency SLOs.
[00:02:50] Ravi Patel: Can you explain adaptive batching briefly?
[00:02:53] Diego Alvarez: Sure — runtime holds requests in a micro-queue for 1–8ms to batch them into a bigger GPU kernel run. For short latency targets we minimize batch delay; for throughput we trade a bit more queuing. We can tune per-route policies: strict latency SLOs will essentially use batch size 1 or small micro-batches.
[00:03:07] Sasha Green: That helps. What about streaming token/sec? For long notes we need sustained 100–200 tokens/sec aggregate across the fleet during peak.
[00:03:15] Diego Alvarez: Streaming throughput depends on model token generation rate and GPU species. For example, on an A100 node a 13B quantized model can sustain ~40–60 tokens/sec single stream; with 8 streams concurrently you get aggregate ~300–400 tokens/sec, subject to kernel parallelism and KV cache efficiency. But quantization and kernel choice will change that.
[00:03:33] Omar Rahman: We're also concerned about p95 when you have a mixture of short and long requests. Does Redwood support priority routing or QoS?
[00:03:41] Maya Chen: Yes — we can pin critical short-completion routes to a low-latency pool and route longer streaming jobs to a separate pool. You can also set fallback policies so if Dedicated runs low on capacity we spill into Hosted variants with lower guarantees.
[00:03:55] Lena Park: On security: we need to confirm VPC peering, private link options, and KMS integration for model input encryption. Also audit logs for every token request for compliance.
[00:04:04] Tom Brooks: We support customer VPCs for Private deployments with a private control plane or VPC peering for Dedicated. KMS/HSM integrations are available so you can retain control of keys. We also provide detailed request-level audit logs with redaction controls.
[00:04:17] Ravi Patel: How does observability impact latency? If we trace every token will that slow things?
[00:04:21] Diego Alvarez: Good question. Token-level tracing is capture-throughput heavy but it's asynchronous — it won't block inference path. However, if you enable synchronous debug traces it will. You can enable sampling or request-level metadata only for production.
[00:04:32] Sasha Green: For our benchmarking, can you simulate network conditions? We have clinics in US-central and west coast and want region-aware numbers.
[00:04:39] Diego Alvarez: We'll run tests from multiple egress regions to simulate cross-region. For Hosted we recommend deploying to the same region as your clients. For Dedicated we can provision multi-region pools or replicate.
[00:04:49] Lena Park: Let's talk numbers: Diego, what's a realistic p95 we can expect for 40-token completion on a tuned 7b in-hosted?
[00:04:56] Diego Alvarez: On edge-optimized infra with batching minimized and region proximity, p95 could be roughly 150–350ms depending on network and cold vs warm. For sustained 200 concurrency we see p95 degrade if you don't reserve capacity. So Dedicated with pinned GPUs gets you consistent p95 ~180–260ms.
[00:05:12] Omar Rahman: If you quote p95 ranges that's helpful — can you also provide p99 for us to understand worst tails?
[00:05:18] Diego Alvarez: Yes I'll include p99. Typically p99 will be 2x–4x p95 due to GC, scheduling, and cold starts unless you mitigate with pre-warming.
[00:05:26] Maya Chen: We'll include warm-up strategies and pre-warm autoscaling knobs in the recommendations. Also prefix/KV caching can reduce token generation work for many of your clinician prompts if they reuse templates.
[00:05:36] Ravi Patel: On the cost side: how much does lower-latency Dedicated cost vs Hosted per token?
[00:05:40] Maya Chen: We'll produce a cost model. Usually Dedicated has a fixed commitment plus lower per-token serving cost at scale. Hosted is more elastic but higher per-token. For strict SLOs Dedicated is generally more predictable. We'll include a sample spreadsheet mapping concurrency -> cost/SLO.
[00:05:53] Lena Park: Can Redwood do A/B routing? Like route 80% to smaller model and 20% to larger to validate quality?
[00:05:59] Priya Nair: Yes, rollouts and canary policies are built in — you can A/B by model version, by route, or by percentage. We can also run automatic fallback if quality metrics degrade.
[00:06:08] Omar Rahman: For the microbenchmark execution: Diego, will you include tests for quantized int8 paths and 4-bit kernels? Some of our perf folks insist on 4-bit numbers.
[00:06:17] Diego Alvarez: Yup — I plan to run q4f16 and int8 where supported, and measure tokens/sec and memory. Quantization often increases throughput but can impact latency variance. I'll annotate results with accuracy delta estimates.
[00:06:29] Sasha Green: Accuracy deltas — how do you measure? Perplexity? Task-level eval?
[00:06:33] Diego Alvarez: We'll include a small prompt set representative of your use-case and report BLEU/ROUGE-ish metrics or token-level similarity; it's not a full eval but gives a signal if quantization materially changes outputs for your prompts.
[00:06:44] Maya Chen: Also to stress test concurrency we'll run synthetic arrival patterns reflecting your 10-minute clinic peaks and steady baseline. That helps size the Dedicated pool.
[00:06:53] Lena Park: When do you think we'll get the spreadsheet?
[00:06:56] Diego Alvarez: I'll aim for EOD 2025-03-17. We have to test across model variants and regions so it takes a couple days.
[00:07:03] Maya Chen: Action items recap coming up. Before that, any other compliance blockers?
[00:07:07] Omar Rahman: We may need an addendum for HIPAA - are you HIPAA-ready?
[00:07:11] Tom Brooks: Redwood has HIPAA-compatible offerings and we have enterprise contracts and BAAs. We'll surface the legal steps and a sample BAA in the security package.
[00:07:20] Ravi Patel: Great. Also, do you log full prompt text by default? We need redaction to avoid PHI leakage in logs.
[00:07:26] Tom Brooks: We provide configurable log retention and redaction; you can opt out of storing raw inputs and instead store hashes or token counts. We'll include configuration options.
[00:07:35] Lena Park: Perfect. One more technical: when you say KV cache, is that per-request or shared across sessions?
[00:07:40] Diego Alvarez: KV cache is per model shard per GPU — so session-specific keys are stored in the GPU KV cache per session for autoregressive decoding. We support prefix caching where common prefixes across requests can be cached and reused if you enable prefix caching, which reduces work for templated prompts.
[00:07:54] Sasha Green: That could drastically help our templated triage prompts. We'll try to provide a sample template.
[00:07:59] Maya Chen: Ok, recap of next steps and action items: Diego will run microbenchmarks (streaming/non-streaming, various quant modes) and share a spreadsheet; Maya will send security docs and BAA; Omar to share traffic profile; we'll schedule a private deployment deep-dive.
[00:08:13] Ravi Patel: Sounds good. Can we schedule the deep-dive for next Tue 09:00 PT?
[00:08:17] Maya Chen: I'll propose that in a calendar invite after the call.
[00:08:21] Lena Park: Thanks everyone — this was helpful.
[00:08:24] Maya Chen: Thanks, we'll follow up with the artifacts. Bye.
[00:08:27] [call ended]
